analysis.one_liner: Makes it much harder for investors to sue companies and executives over securities fraud.
analysis.headline: Congress passed the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995 over President Clinton's veto — the House voted 325-99 to pass it and 319-100 to override the veto, and the Senate voted 69-30 and 68-30.
analysis.plain_summary: This law rewrote the rules for private securities fraud lawsuits, the main way ordinary shareholders — including people holding stock through retirement plans — can recover money when a company lies about its finances or prospects. It requires far more detailed proof before a case can even get going, pauses evidence-gathering while defendants try to get cases thrown out, caps damages, protects company forecasts from being used as the basis for a lawsuit, and limits how much any one defendant has to pay. It also added protections against some abusive lawsuit practices and new auditor duties to detect and report corporate fraud.
analysis.who_benefits: Publicly traded companies and their executives, directors, and auditors gain the most: they face far fewer and cheaper shareholder lawsuits, a safe harbor for optimistic projections, protection from being held responsible for another party's full share of damages, and lower damages overall. Plaintiff attorneys lose business, but the people whose money was at stake — defrauded shareholders — also lose a major tool for recovering losses.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Public companies, executives, and audit firms

how_it_helps.text: Companies facing shareholder suits can now get a case dismissed unless the complaint states specific facts showing the defendants acted knowingly, and courts must dismiss cases that fall short [S5].
Evidence-gathering is frozen while a motion to dismiss is pending, so defendants avoid the pre-trial discovery costs that often pushed companies toward early settlements [S5] [S6].

Executives get a 'safe harbor' protecting them from liability over forward-looking statements like earnings projections, as long as the statement is identified as such and accompanied by cautionary language [S5] [S6].

Defendants who did not knowingly commit a violation are liable only for their own percentage of responsibility rather than the full judgment, and outside directors are shielded from joint and several liability [S5] [S6].
Damages are capped, generally at the difference between what the shareholder paid and the stock's average price during the 90 days after the truth came out [S5].
The law removes securities fraud from the scope of the RICO statute's treble-damages provision, except where a participant in the fraud is criminally convicted [S5].

analysis.who_pays: Investors who lose money to securities fraud — including people with 401(k)s, pensions, and mutual funds — bear the cost, because the law makes it substantially harder and more expensive for a shareholder class action to survive and recover money. Plaintiff attorneys also lose, but the recovery that would have flowed to shareholders is the real cost.

drawbacks.text: Supporters argued the law targeted real abuses: professional plaintiffs who filed many suits, lawyers who collected large fees while class members received little, and defendants pressured into paying coercive settlements to avoid ruinous joint liability. The bill's own findings cite securities fraud aimed at senior citizens and retirement plans, and it directs the SEC to study whether they need more protection under the new rules [S4] [S5] [S6].

The bill includes genuine investor-protection provisions: auditors must adopt procedures to detect illegal acts and report them up the chain and to the SEC, settlement terms must be disclosed to class members, and brokers may no longer take referral fees for steering clients to securities lawyers [S4] [S5] [S6].

The strongest cost an honest supporter had to acknowledge: the heightened pleading standards, the stay on discovery, and the cap on damages apply not only to frivolous suits but to meritorious ones, because a legitimate fraud case often cannot be proved without the discovery that is now blocked until the complaint survives dismissal. The Senate-passed bill itself acknowledged SEC concern with some provisions [S4] [S6].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Some of this law helps ordinary investors: cracking down on professional plaintiffs, exposing secret settlements, requiring settlement disclosure, and forcing auditors to look for and report corporate fraud are real benefits. But the core of the law — the pleading hurdles, the freeze on discovery, the safe harbor for projections, the damage caps, and the end of joint liability for unknowing defendants — shifted the risk of corporate fraud away from companies and executives and onto the shareholders who bought their stock. On balance, a shareholder defrauded by a company has much less ability to recover than before, and the class action that was already hard to win became harder still.

outcome.mechanism: It passed both chambers by wide margins, President Clinton vetoed it saying it went too far, and both chambers voted again the same week to pass it over his objection, making it law.

narrative.text: The House passed the bill on March 8, 1995, 325-99, with 226 of 230 Republicans voting yes and Democrats split 99-98 [S10].
A Democratic motion to recommit the bill with amendments protecting investors failed 172-251, with 169 of 204 Democrats for it and 224 of 229 Republicans against [S9].
The Senate passed it on June 28, 1995, 69-30: 49 of 54 Republicans yes, and Democrats split 20-26 [S11].
After a House-Senate conference negotiated the final version, the Senate agreed to the conference report 65-30 on December 5 and the House 320-102 on December 6 [S12] [S13].
President Clinton vetoed the bill on December 19, 1995 [S8].
The House overrode the veto 319-100 on December 20 (two-thirds required) and the Senate followed 68-30 on December 22; the bill became Public Law 104-67 [S14] [S15] [S8].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Publicly traded companies and their executives, directors, and auditors came out ahead: they got the liability protections they had sought for years, over a presidential veto. Defrauded shareholders, including retirement savers, came out with a much harder path to recovering losses, though they did gain the auditor fraud-reporting and settlement-disclosure provisions.

for.name: Rep. Tom Bliley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded it through the House, then brought the conference report to the floor and managed the veto override.

for.name: 230 of 230 House Republicans voting
for.what_they_did: Voted unanimously for passage, for the conference report, and for the veto override.

for.name: 49 of 54 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Voted overwhelmingly for the bill (49-4), for the conference report (46-4), and to override the veto (48-4).

for.name: Securities industry and accounting firms
for.role: Corporate issuers, executives, and audit firms
for.what_they_did: Lobbied for years for limits on securities fraud lawsuits; proportionate liability and the safe harbor were long-standing industry priorities.

for.name: Speaker Newt Gingrich
for.what_they_did: Brought the bill to the floor under rules allowing quick consideration and presided over the chamber as it passed and overrode the veto.

against.name: President Bill Clinton
against.what_they_did: Vetoed the bill on December 19, 1995, arguing it undermined investor protection; his veto was overridden within days.

against.name: 101 of 197 House Democrats
against.what_they_did: Voted against the conference report and 99 voted to sustain the veto; roughly half the party's House members backed the bill on final passage.

against.name: Rep. John Dingell
against.what_they_did: Offered investor-protective amendments that were incorporated in a motion to recommit; that motion failed 172-251.

against.name: Rep. Edward Markey
against.what_they_did: Moved to recommit the bill with instructions to add the Dingell and Manton amendments before final passage.

against.name: Securities and Exchange Commission
against.what_they_did: Expressed concern with the bill's provisions; the Senate version itself directed the SEC to recommend added protections for seniors and retirement plans.

sides.party_line_note: Republicans were nearly unanimous throughout — 226-0 in the House on passage and 49-4 and 48-4 in the Senate on passage and the override — while Democrats split close to evenly, with most House Democrats voting no on the final version (101-90) and a narrow majority of Senate Democrats voting no (26-20).

industries.industry: Publicly traded companies and their executives and directors
industries.note: The law sharply raises the bar for shareholders to sue them for fraud: detailed pleading, a freeze on discovery, a safe harbor for projections, damages caps, and liability limited to each defendant's own share. The main enforcement mechanism against corporate misstatements that hit ordinary retirement savers and small investors was weakened.

The law caps their exposure at their own proportionate share of damages rather than full joint liability, their top priority. In exchange they took on new duties to detect and report illegal acts found in audits, with SEC penalties for failing to report.

Sanctions for inadequate complaints, a presumptive award of defendants' legal fees, mandatory dismissal of weak pleadings, and the discovery freeze sharply reduce the number and profitability of cases. Ordinary investors lose the recovery these cases produced.

The lead-plaintiff provision favors the investor with the largest financial stake becoming lead plaintiff, which large pension funds later used to take control of class actions from law firms. But the same funds' members face a harder path to recovering fraud losses.
The law bans brokers from taking referral fees for steering clients to securities lawyers — a practice that funneled investors' own lawsuit business toward particular firms.
